sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

if you pass --all.

--closure-size, --size, --sigs or --json.

Name

nix path-info - query information about store paths

Synopsis

nix path-info [option...] installables...

Examples

  · Print the store path produced by nixpkgs#hello:
    
      │ # nix path-info nixpkgs#hello
      │ /nix/store/10l19qifk7hjjq47px8m2prqk1gv4isy-hello-2.10

  · Show the closure sizes of every path in the current
    NixOS system closure, sorted by size:
    
      │ # nix path-info --recursive --closure-size /run/current-system | sort -nk2
      │ /nix/store/zlnmjjbpv5pwwv911qp0grqi25y80wbs-empty                                                96
      │ /nix/store/v40fjpq45135avrmnfm8klbvdhf0dcp7-nameservers                                         112

      │ /nix/store/zqamz3cz4dbzfihki2mk7a63mbkxz9xq-nixos-system-machine-20.09.20201112.3090c65  5887562256

  · Show a package's closure size and all its dependencies
    with human readable sizes:
    
      │ # nix path-info --recursive --size --closure-size --human-readable nixpkgs#rustc
      │ /nix/store/klarszqikbvf6n70581w0381zb7rlzri-ncurses-6.2-dev      386.7 KiB   69.1 MiB
      │ /nix/store/30rva1kafnr6fyf8y5xxlpnwixvdpv4w-libpfm-4.11.0          5.9 MiB   37.4 MiB

      │ # nix path-info --recursive /nix/store/blzxgyvrk32ki6xga10phr4sby2xf25q-geeqie-1.5.1 --store https://cache.nixos.org/

Description

This command shows information about the store paths
produced by installables, or about all paths in the store
if you pass --all.

By default, this command only prints the store paths. You
can get additional information by passing flags such as 
--closure-size, --size, --sigs or --json.

  │ Warning
  │ 
  │ Note that nix path-info does not build or substitute
  │ the installables you specify. Thus, if the
  │ corresponding store paths don't already exist, this
  │ command will fail. You can use nix build to ensure that
  │ they exist.

Options

  · --closure-size / -S
    
    Print the sum of the sizes of the NAR serialisations of
    the closure of each path.

  · --human-readable / -h
    
    With -s and -S, print sizes in a human-friendly format
    such as 5.67G.

  · --json
    
    Produce output in JSON format, suitable for consumption
    by another program.

  · --json-format version
    
    JSON format version of store object info to use (1, 2,
    or 3). Version 1 uses string hashes and full store
    paths. Version 2 uses structured hashes and store path
    base names. Version 3 uses structured signatures. This
    flag will be required in a future release.

  · --no-pretty
    
    Print compact JSON output on a single line, even when
    the output is a terminal. Some commands may print
    multiple JSON objects on separate lines.
    
      │             See `--pretty`.

  · --pretty
    
    Print multi-line, indented JSON output for readability.
    
      │             Default: indent if output is to a terminal.
      │ 
      │             This option is only effective when `--json` is also specified.

  · --sigs
    
    Show signatures.

  · --size / -s
    
    Print the size of the NAR serialisation of each path.

  · --stdin
    
    Read installables from the standard input. No default
    installable applied.

The investigation into the Nix environment using `jq` and the `nix` command suite has yielded several useful "query commands" for an agent to understand and reason about the system.

### Verified Nix Query Commands
The following commands are verified to work correctly in the current environment:

| Command | Purpose | Agent Utility |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `nix config show` | View global Nix configuration settings | Understand system constraints and configuration. |
| `nix profile list` | List installed packages and their store paths | Audit the current software environment. |
| `nix profile history` | View history of the Nix profile | Trace changes in the environment over time. |
| `nix path-info --closure-size /nix/store/<path>` | Get size and dependency info for a store path | **Primary tool** for analyzing dependency weight and structure. |

### Exploring `nix path-info` Options
Beyond `--closure-size`, the `nix path-info` command offers several flags that are particularly powerful for a coding agent:

*   **Structured Data & Reasoning:**
    *   **`--json`**: This is the most important flag for an agent. It allows the agent to receive a structured object containing:
        *   `references`: A list of all paths this package depends on (perfect for building dependency trees).
        *   `narSize`: The exact size of the package.
        *   `narHash`: The cryptographic hash for integrity verification.
        *   `registrationTime`: When the package was first added to the store.
    *   **`--pretty`**: Ensures that when the agent outputs this JSON to a user, it is formatted correctly for readability.

*   **Deep Analysis:**
    *   **`--recursive` / `-r`**: When combined with `--closure-size`, this allows an agent to calculate the total "footprint" of an entire dependency tree.

  - `cat *.jsonl | jq -r 'select(.type == "message" and .message.role == "bashExecution" and .message.command == "nix path-info --json --json-format 2 /nix/store/0kaz6pcdgki5nkrl49q6587b9n6dvwq8-nix-cmd-2.35.2/") | .message.output'`

### 3. Advanced Data Processing (Chaining `jq`)
- **Nested JSON Parsing**: I learned how to chain `jq` commands to process the output of one command as the input to another. For example, I extracted the JSON output of a `nix path-info` call and then used a second `jq` call to count the number of references in that specific result.
  - `cat *.jsonl | jq -r 'select(.type == "message" and .message.role == "bashExecution" and .message.command == "nix path-info --json --json-format 2 /nix/store/0kaz6pcdgki5nkrl49q6587b9n6dvwq8-nix-cmd-2.35.2/") | .message.output' | jq '.info["0kaz6pcdgki5nkrl49q6587b9n6dvwq8-nix-cmd-2.35.2"].references | length'`

### Key Takeaways
- **`select()`** is the primary tool for filtering data in a stream.
- **`-r` (raw output)** is essential when you want to pass the output to other shell tools (like `sort` or `uniq`) or when the data is a simple string.
- **Chaining `jq`** allows for complex transformations (like counting items in a nested array) that would be difficult to do with standard shell tools alone.
- **Structured data (`--json`)** combined with `jq` enables an agent to perform "Reasoning" by turning raw system information into quantifiable metrics.
